points.t: An expanding red (or bluish) patch days to weeks after outdoor exposure — central clearing is optional, and itch/heat are usually mild.
Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato from an Ixodes tick spreads in the dermis (EM) or persists chronically (ACA, mainly European B. afzelii).
EM: doxycycline 100 mg BD (or 200 mg OD) for 21 days. No blood test needed for typical EM.
Carditis, meningitis/encephalitis, uveitis, or facial palsy with focal neurology — emergency or same-day pathways. Do not test or give antibiotics after an asymptomatic bite.

points: Vector: hard tick ***Ixodes ricinus*** (sheep/deer tick). Tiny nymphs cause most infections. **Most bites do not transmit**; risk rises after about 24–48 hours of attachment, so prompt correct removal helps (NICE NG95).
UK risk: grassy/wooded areas, parks and gardens — higher in southern England and the Scottish Highlands, but possible anywhere. Peak spring–autumn.
EM: dermal spread from the bite. Dissemination can cause multiple EM, neuroborreliosis, carditis and arthritis.
ACA: chronic skin infection on acral extensors, often without a remembered bite.
A **red rash that enlarges** over days; may have central clearing (“bull’s-eye”), but many lesions are uniformly red or bluish.
Usually **not** hot, itchy or painful. Appears **3 days to 3 months** after a bite (commonly 1–4 weeks).
Often ≥5 cm at the bite site (legs, groin, axillae, beltline; head/neck in children). Harder to see in darker skin (bruise-like).
**Inflammatory stage:** bluish-red doughy discolouration of an extensor limb (hand, forearm, lower leg), often unilateral.
**Atrophic stage:** thin “cigarette-paper” skin with visible veins — easily mistaken for ageing or venous disease.
diagnose or test after an asymptomatic tick bite.
**EM: diagnose and treat clinically. No blood test** — early serology is often negative (NG95).
Without EM (including suspected ACA): clinical picture plus **ELISA then immunoblot** via a UKAS-accredited lab. ACA is nearly always strongly IgG-positive.
Do not rely on private “Lyme specialty” panels without checking accreditation.
Absence of a remembered bite does **not** exclude Lyme.

cards.name: Tick-bite hypersensitivity
cards.clue: Hours onset, fades ≤48 h, itchy/hot, small

cards.name: Tinea corporis
cards.clue: Scaly active edge; EM is not scaly

cards.name: Granuloma annulare
cards.clue: Chronic firm papule ring; no day-by-day expansion

cards.name: ACA mimics
cards.clue: Chilblains, venous disease, morphoea, ageing skin — check exposure and serology

items.t: Emergency pathways even if Lyme is possible: meningitis/encephalitis signs, uveitis, carditis or complete heart block.
Same-day/urgent GP: facial palsy, radiculopathy, inflammatory arthritis, multiple EM with systemic upset — discuss with a specialist without delaying antibiotics.
Persistent symptoms after two completed antibiotic courses: do not give more antibiotics; seek specialist/reference-lab advice.

pearls.t: **Expanding red ring after the outdoors = treat. Don’t test.**
Draw round the edge and photograph to monitor spread.
A full **21-day** course matters for EM.
Reinfection is possible — infection does not confer lasting immunity.
ACA is often missed as “poor circulation” in an older person’s limb — ask about European countryside exposure and test.
